title: VPC Segmentation & PrivateLink runtime + KV cache deep-dive
summary: Deep technical discussion covering PrivateLink wiring for Redwood Private in a segmented VPC architecture, hairpin NAT risks for cross-subnet KV cache access, DNS/resolver patterns (split-horizon, Route53 inbound), and runtime performance tradeoffs (batching windows, quantization profiles) for a pilot. Agreed next steps: send networking runbook, share PoC infra template, schedule pilot provisioning, and run a short latency benchmark with KV cache enabled.

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-08-27 15:30 UTC | Duration: ~65m
Attendees: Alex Perez (Redwood AE), Samir Rao (Redwood SE), Janelle Wu (Redwood SE), Morgan Ellis (NimbleHealth), Priya Shah (NimbleHealth), Diego Alvarez (NimbleHealth)

[00:00] Alex (AE): Hey everyone thanks for joining, we wanted to run through the network wiring and a few runtime perf knobs so the pilot is low risk. Quick check — is the timeline still target early September for the PoC?
[00:18] Morgan (Platform Eng): Yep that's right, we're aiming to have a sandbox VPC up by the first week of September. We want to validate performance with KV cache on and one of your quantized models.
[00:32] Samir (SE): Great. I'll cover the PrivateLink topology we recommend, then Janelle and I will dig into KV cache reachability and the hairpin concerns.
[00:45] Priya (Security): Quick note — we need to keep all egress restricted and use our KMS for key wrapping. Also SOC2 and data residency questions will come up in the questionnaire you sent.
[01:05] Alex (AE): Noted — we'll attach the security pack. Samir, over to you for the diagram.
[01:12] Samir (SE): Ok so recommended pattern: a dedicated subnet for Redwood Private endpoints, PrivateLink endpoints (interface endpoints) in the customer VPC, a pair of subnets for the model workers behind a separate route table, and a minimal egress NAT for software updates. The important bit is we advise interface endpoints (PrivateLink) instead of open internet egress for control plane calls.
[01:38] Samir (SE): In a segmented VPC you want isolation between prod-like subnets and sandbox. Use security groups referencing endpoint IDs, not just IP prefixes, that reduces accidental wide-open SGs.
[01:54] Morgan (Customer): A question — our infra team wanted to put Redwood on a different account and cross-account PrivateLink was mentioned. Does that change anything for KV cache routing?
[02:07] Janelle (SE): Cross-account PrivateLink is fine for the control plane. For the data plane — especially KV cache traffic from inference workers to a caching tier — we recommend same-account peering or Transit Gateway to avoid hairpin NAT because hairpin adds latency and breaks keepalives in some runtimes.
[02:29] Diego (SRE): Could you say more about the hairpin NAT failure modes? We've seen weird TCP resets when traffic goes out through egress and back in.
[02:38] Samir (SE): Yeah. If the worker pod's route sends to a NAT Gateway and the NAT path returns to the same subnet via the internet gateway/egress path, you can hit asymmetric routing. That breaks connection tracking on the NAT and causes resets; with a KV cache that maintains long-lived TCP/KV sessions that's bad. We prefer direct routing via TGW or VPC peering so the ENI never hairpins.
[03:05] Priya (Customer): So does Redwood require that KV cache be reachable from the same subnet as the worker?
[03:11] Samir (SE): Not necessarily same subnet but within a deterministic path — same VPC and private routing, ideally same AZ to avoid cross-AZ latency. We support cross-subnet but you can't put a forced egress through NAT for cache traffic.
[03:28] Alex (AE): What about split-horizon DNS? We plan to use internal hostnames for endpoints.
[03:36] Janelle (SE): Split-horizon is common — customer resolver returns private interface endpoint addresses. A common pitfall: if you have an egress resolver (proxy) that rewrites DNS, it can return public addresses and then traffic misroutes. So ensure the VPC resolver/Route53 inbound zones resolve to endpoint IPs.
[03:58] Morgan: We use Route53 inbound for on-prem to VPC name resolution, will that interfere?
[04:05] Samir: Fine if it's configured as split-horizon; just verify TTLs and test from an instance in the target subnet. Also add an A record for the kv-cache cluster with multi-AZ IPs.
[04:18] Diego: How does Redwood Private authenticate to KV cache? We run Redis with TLS client certs.
[04:25] Samir: We can support mutual TLS and token-based auth. For TLS client certs you'll need to ensure the worker nodes have the certs via secure secrets (SSM or Vault). If you're using a managed Redis, the same approach applies.
[04:40] Priya: And KMS? We require use of our CMK for any customer data keys.
[04:46] Alex: Redwood Private supports customer-managed keys (HSM/KMS). We'll add the KMS stub to the security doc for you.

[05:02] Samir: Switching to runtime perf — short primer: latency SLOs are a function of model size, quantization, batch size, and cache hit rate. With an effective KV cache hit rate >85% you see token-latency improvements because prefix KV avoids recomputation.
[05:22] Janelle: Important runtime knobs: continuous batching window (we default to 8ms for latency-sensitive and 40ms for throughput), max_batch_size, and prefetch for KV requests. The prefetch controls K/V pipelining so you don't block the token generation pipeline.
[05:42] Morgan: If we use a 40ms batching window to save cost, will our p95 latency blow up? We need p95 < 250ms.
[05:50] Janelle: For small requests (<=32 tokens) a 40ms window plus batch size 16 can still meet p95 under 250ms if the model is quantized to q4_0 or int8. But the back-and-forth for KV reads adds ~10-30ms depending on AZ. So aim for 20-30ms batching window for p95 safety if KV hits aren't perfect.
[06:12] Samir: Note: quantization 8-bit vs 4-bit — q4_0 gives good perf/cost tradeoff; q2/q4/fp16 differences depend on workload. We'll share benchmarks.
[06:24] Diego: Are there any runtime crash modes when KV cache connectivity flaps?
[06:29] Samir: Good question — Redwood runtime is resilient: it degrades to model-only generation if cache is unreachable, but you should avoid flapping because cold-start penalty is high. We provide circuit-breaker settings: fail-open vs fail-closed. For your use case we recommended fail-open with retry/backoff.

[06:50] Alex: On the networking side, a few concrete patterns we saw: (1) PrivateLink control-plane + same-account TGW for data-plane, (2) Service mesh sidecar with egress rules pinned to endpoint IPs, (3) dedicated cache ENIs per AZ.
[07:08] Priya: We use a strict proxy for outbound egress — everything must go through our outbound proxy. Is that incompatible with PrivateLink?
[07:16] Samir: Not incompatible, but you must exclude PrivateLink interface endpoints from proxy rules or ensure proxy can reach the private endpoints directly. If the proxy rewrites SNI or terminates TLS you may break mTLS to the cache.
[07:33] Morgan: For cross-account PrivateLink, do you recommend VPC endpoint services in Redwood account or the other way around?
[07:41] Samir: Typically customer owns the endpoint in their account and we provide the service name; cross-account acceptance just needs the principal in endpoint policy. For managed infra, some customers prefer Redwood to host the endpoint service in our account and customer connects — that is operationally heavier. We can support both.

[08:05] Janelle: Let's walk through a failure scenario — suppose NAT is used and KV cache IPs route out and back in. Latency spikes and connection resets. The mitigation: add a route to point to the private target ENI or TGW and tighten security groups. Also set TCP keepalive lower so application detects drops faster.
[08:25] Diego: What about MTU and packet fragmentation with PrivateLink? We've hit issues with jumbo frames.
[08:31] Samir: Ensure MTU is consistent across peering/TGW; PrivateLink and ENIs pass through the usual 1500 by default. If you enable jumbo frames, confirm all segments support it. Fragmentation increases latency unpredictably.

[08:50] Alex: Quick perf numbers from our lab: baseline p50 token latency 18ms with q4_0, batch size 8, continuous 8ms window; p95 210ms with KV hit rate 90%. With 40ms window and batch 32 you can reduce cost per token ~2.5x but p95 moves to ~380ms. We can share the full CSV.
[09:15] Morgan: We'll need that CSV to decide which latency/cost config to pick for prod.
[09:19] Alex: Yep — we'll include model-specific curves.

[09:28] Priya: On audit logs — we need per-request logs and redaction. Does Redwood capture full prompts in logs?
[09:36] Alex: We provide configurable logging: you can redact PII and keep metadata for traces. For enterprise we support long-term log retention in your S3 and integration with Splunk.
[09:48] Priya: Great. Also can Redwood run in our air-gapped environment if needed?
[09:53] Samir: We have an on-prem package with an isolated control plane; networking is more manual there but doable. For this pilot we'll use Private VPC deployment.

[10:05] Janelle: Practical checklist for the pilot: create dedicated subnets for endpoints and workers; attach route table entries so cache traffic uses peering/TGW; ensure DNS resolves to private IPs; whitelist Redwood service principal in endpoint policy; provision KMS keys; create service account and secrets for TLS certs.
[10:25] Morgan: Sounds good. One practical item: we use an egress NAT for software patching — can we keep that but exclude the cache CIDR?
[10:33] Samir: Yes exclude the cache CIDR and ensure route table has more specific route to cache. That prevents hairpin.

[10:42] Diego: On the runtime: what's the recommended max_batch_size for our 8GB GPU workers?
[10:47] Janelle: Typical guidance: for smaller models with q4_0 on 8GB, max_batch_size 16–24 is reasonable, continuous window 8–20ms for latency targets. If you want heavy throughput consider bumping to 40ms and max_batch 64 but that needs larger GPU.
[11:04] Morgan: Can Redwood's autoscaler scale worker pools per AZ? We want to avoid cross-AZ traffic for cache reads.
[11:10] Samir: Yes, autoscaler is AZ-aware and you can pin pools per AZ. We also support placement constraints so workers only schedule in specific subnets.

[11:22] Alex: I'll recap then — networking: avoid hairpin NAT, prefer TGW/peering, PrivateLink for control plane, ensure split-horizon DNS; runtime: aim for q4_0 quantization, 8–20ms batching window for latency, use KV cache with prefetch and fail-open.
[11:42] Priya: For the security questionnaire, what exact artifacts will you provide?
[11:46] Alex: We'll share SOC2 summary, KMS/HSM integration notes, endpoint policies, and the networking runbook (diagram + Terraform PoC).
[11:55] Morgan: Ok let's set a concrete date for pilot kickoff — how about 2026-09-08?
[12:00] Alex: I'll put a calendar invite for 2026-09-08 and include the infra checklist and sample terraform.

[12:07] Diego: One last perf nuance — if KV cache is hit/miss mixed we should instrument token-level latency, can Redwood emit token latencies per request?
[12:15] Janelle: Yes token-level traces via the console and tracing hooks. We can also export to OpenTelemetry.

[12:25] Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the runbook and PoC + pricing estimate. Any final quick Qs?
[12:31] Priya: Nothing else. Thanks.
[12:33] Morgan: Thanks team.

[12:35] (call ends)

Notes: Transcript includes occasional mislabels and real-world pauses. Some technical jargon may be slightly mistranscribed (e.g., hairpin sometimes appears as "hair pin").
